docs.text:
⬢ public hub agentic tooling, symlinked

01 · The stack

One repo. One symlink pass.

The installer does not copy files. It links them, so a git pull updates every harness in place.

26 skillsskills/One SKILL.md each, symlinked into ~/.claude/skills/. 10+ scriptsworkflows/.mjs coordinators for the Workflow tool. 5 runtimesharnesses/Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Hermes. terminalconfig/tmux, zsh fragments, statusline. installersetup/Component picker and variable templating.

02 · Signature loop

Nothing merges unopposed.

The council is the spine of this repo. Advocates argue for the change, critics argue against it, a Socratic questioner probes both, and an arbiter issues a verdict. Fix rounds run until the verdict is unconditional.

01BrainstormOne question at a time until the design is approved. 02SpecGherkin scenarios and MoSCoW scope, section by section. 03ImplementTasks routed to subagents in dependency-aware waves. 04CouncilAdvocates, critics, questioner, arbiter. Verdict or fix round. 05MergeSquash, advance to the next sibling branch, repeat.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text: Adopt the hub in layers. Each layer works without the next, and each layer builds the habits the next layer assumes. Do not install everything on day one. This tier gets you your first productive session: install, a durable tmux session, and a first skill run. Start here even if you already know Claude Code, because the tmux keybindings and the skill names are specific to this hub.

docs.title: Install Claude Code
docs.text:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
Expected outcome: the claude command is on your PATH.

claude --version
Expected outcome: prints a version string, for example 2.x.x (Claude Code).

docs.title: Install the GitHub CLI
docs.text:
The GitHub CLI handles auth for the clone, so a fresh machine needs no SSH alias and no manual key setup.

pacman -S github-cli   # Arch. macOS: brew install gh. Debian: apt install gh
Expected outcome: the gh command is on your PATH.

gh auth login
Expected outcome: an interactive login. Pick github.com, then SSH or HTTPS, and finish in the browser. Run this once per machine.

docs.title: Clone the hub
docs.text:
gh repo clone Kiriketsuki/agenKic-hub
cd agenKic-hub
Expected outcome: the repo sits at agenKic-hub/ in your current directory.

docs.title: Run the installer
docs.text:
./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: an interactive picker starts. It lists every component manifest under setup/components/, one line per component with its description. Select skills-core and config-tmux for this tier, then answer the template prompts that follow (accept the defaults on your first run).

./setup/setup.sh --dry-run
Expected outcome: prints every action the picker's selection would take, with no change on disk. Run this first if you want to preview before you commit.

For a non-interactive run, copy setup/answers.example.yml, edit the components: line and the template variables, then pass it back in:

./setup/setup.sh --profile setup/answers.yml
Expected outcome: the same install runs with no prompts.

Windows users run pwsh setup/setup.ps1 instead, then follow the rest of this walkthrough as written documentation, since setup/walkthrough.sh covers Linux and macOS only.

docs.title: The four skill groups
docs.text:
Skills sit under skills/ in four groups. Each group has its own manifest under setup/components/, so the picker offers them one at a time, and each selection symlinks that group's skills individually into ~/.claude/skills/.

Group Manifest Skills Buys you skills/core/ skills-core.conf brainstorm, brainstorm-grill, feature-spec, implement-spec, merge-next, context-handoff, context-resume, agent-route, model-route The spec-first loop this tier's capstone runs skills/council/ skills-council.conf adversarial-council, council-fix, council-supervisor, parallel-fix Debate a change before it merges, see Advanced skills/writing/ skills-writing.conf ste-writing, kilint, visual-explainer, cover-letter The prose house style, and a linter that checks it skills/ops/ skills-ops.conf repo-hooks, security-scan, croc-send, release-notes-enricher, insights-to-vault, continuous-learning-v2 Guard rails and repo maintenance

Basics needs only skills-core. Install the rest as Intermediate and Advanced call for them.

docs.title: tmux for agents
docs.text:
Claude Code sessions run inside a shell process. Close the terminal window and the process dies with it. tmux keeps a session running on the machine independent of any one terminal window. An agent keeps working while you disconnect, close your laptop lid, or lose a network link. Reattach later and the session is exactly where you left it.

tmux new -s hub
Expected outcome: a new tmux session named hub opens, with a status bar at the bottom.

Start Claude Code inside that session, then detach without killing it:

Ctrl+a d
Expected outcome: you return to your normal shell. The session, and any agent running inside it, keeps running in the background.

tmux attach -t hub
Expected outcome: you land back inside the same session, with the agent's output exactly as you left it.

The hub renders config/tmux/tmux.conf.tmpl into ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf during setup. The prefix is Ctrl+a, nearer your home row than the default Ctrl+b.

docs.title: The command palette
docs.text:
Ctrl+a Space
Expected outcome: a floating command palette opens, an fzf picker over 51 tmux actions from config/tmux/scripts/palette.sh. Type to filter, Enter to run, Esc to cancel. Requires fzf on your PATH. When fzf is absent, the palette prints an install hint instead of opening.

docs.title: First skill run
docs.text:
Open Claude Code inside your tmux session and complete one skill run. Any completed skill run finishes this tier. Any skill from any group works. The guided example below is the spec pair from skills-core, but a /kilint pass on a file or a /security-scan also counts.

/brainstorm
Expected outcome: Claude Code asks clarifying questions about what you want to build, one at a time. It then proposes two or three approaches and asks for your approval.

/feature-spec
Expected outcome: Claude Code interviews you section by section, then writes a filled docs/specs/todo/<feature-name>-spec.md file in the target repo. Run this after /brainstorm approves a design, or on its own for a feature you already understand well.

Basics ends here. You have a working install, a durable tmux session, and one completed skill run.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text: This tier adds the habits that keep any long Claude Code session usable: context management, the rest of the spec loop, and guard-rail hooks. A hook enforces a rule deterministically, so it does not depend on the model remembering the rule.

docs.title: Context management
docs.text:
A long session accumulates conversation history that a model eventually must summarize or lose. The hub gives you two skills that make that transition deliberate instead of automatic.

/context-handoff
Expected outcome: Claude Code writes a handoff file that orients a fresh session. It states the active task, the decisions made and why, the approaches that failed, and the concrete next steps. Run this before /clear or before compaction, not after.

/context-resume active
Expected outcome: Claude Code loads the most recent handoff file, verifies the current git state, and re-reads the key files the handoff names.

Watch the context bar in your session. Work freely below about 50 percent of the window, watch it from 50 to 80 percent, and hand off at about 80 percent. Do not ride the bar into the summarizer, since a forced summary drops the nuance a deliberate handoff keeps.

Three built-in commands help before you reach the limit. Run /compact <instructions> to tell the summarizer what to keep. Run /rewind and choose summarize to compress from a chosen message onward. Run /btw to ask a side question that stays out of the conversation history.

Run /clear between unrelated tasks, not mid-task. A cleared context starts a new conversation with no memory of what came before. Clear only after a handoff exists or after a task fully lands.

docs.title: The full spec loop
docs.text:
The core skills from Basics start the spec-first loop: brainstorm and feature-spec. These two finish it.

/implement-spec
Expected outcome: Claude Code reads a *-spec.md file, routes its tasks to subagents, and executes them in dependency-aware waves, committing after each logical chunk. Point it at a spec in docs/specs/todo/, or let it find the most recent one.

/merge-next
Expected outcome: Claude Code commits any remaining work, pushes, and verifies the pull request targets the correct parent branch. It then squash merges the PR, checks out the next sibling branch, and rebases it onto the parent. Run this when a feature, task, epic, or saga branch is ready to ship.

docs.title: Guard-rail hooks
docs.text:
A hook is a shell command the harness runs around a tool call. It enforces a rule deterministically, without depending on the model remembering an instruction. Install skills-ops for repo-hooks once your core loop feels routine:

./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select skills-ops in the picker. The installer symlinks repo-hooks into ~/.claude/skills/. Run /repo-hooks from any session afterward to wire the guard rails into that repo's .claude/settings.json.

docs.title: Council and writing skills
docs.text:
skills-council and skills-writing add a debate loop and a prose house style on top of the core loop. Install both once the core loop feels routine, since council fix rounds and STE prose both assume the spec loop already works for you.

./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select skills-council and skills-writing in the picker. Both groups symlink into ~/.claude/skills/. Run /kilint on any markdown file, or continue to Advanced for /adversarial-council.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text: The workflow scripts below fan out multiple agents at once. They compose the skills from Basics and Intermediate, so confirm those already work on your machine before you install workflows/.

docs.title: Multi-agent workflows
docs.text:
./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select workflows in the picker. The installer symlinks each workflows/<name> entry into ~/.claude/workflows/<name>, covering spec-loop, feature-loop, council-loop, ultracode-fix, ultracode-implement, and further coordinator scripts for the Workflow tool.

docs.title: Adversarial council
docs.text:
/adversarial-council
Expected outcome: Claude Code convenes a team of real spawned advocate and critic agents to debate a motion. An arbiter moderates the debate and produces a FOR, AGAINST, or CONDITIONAL recommendation with cited rationale.

docs.title: Authoring a new skill
docs.text:
Study an existing skill under skills/core/ before you write your own. Each SKILL.md carries YAML frontmatter with a name, a description that states its trigger phrases, and a body that walks the process step by step. Place a new skill under the group it serves (skills/core/, skills/council/, skills/writing/, or skills/ops/), then add it to that group's manifest under setup/components/ so the installer offers it.

python3 skills/writing/kilint/bin/kilint skills/<group>/<your-skill>/SKILL.md
Expected outcome: a violation score under 1.5 per 100 words. Every skill body follows the same STE house style as the rest of the hub's prose.

docs.title: Extras: the real rice
docs.text: Nothing in this section is required. The three components below install real external repos through the same type=external component path as every other manifest. The installer clones or pulls the repo. It then runs its own installer script, or applies the repo with stow. --dry-run prints the clone-and-run plan for any of them. It makes no change on disk.

docs.title: ext-statusline
docs.text:
./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select ext-statusline in the picker. The installer clones Kiriketsuki/chrysaki-claude to ~/.local/share/chrysaki-claude and runs that repo's own init.sh, which installs the statusline and wires statusLine into ~/.claude/settings.json. Restart Claude Code afterward to see it render.

docs.title: ext-tmux-theme
docs.text:
./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select ext-tmux-theme in the picker. The installer clones Kiriketsuki/chrysaki to ~/.config/tmux/chrysaki. The rendered tmux.conf already carries a guarded source line for the theme file. The theme activates the next time you reload tmux with Ctrl+a r, no edit needed.

docs.title: ext-dots
docs.text:
./setup/setup.sh
Expected outcome: select ext-dots in the picker. The installer clones Kiriketsuki/dots to ~/dots and applies it with stow, symlinking the rest of the dotfiles into your home directory. Follow the dots repo's own README for anything the stow pass does not cover.

docs.title: Authoring Workflow scripts
docs.text:
The Workflow tool runs a plain JavaScript orchestration script in a sandboxed loop. The script sequences subagents, checks their structured returns, and loops until a convergence condition holds. This article distills the authoring patterns from the scripts in this repo's workflows/ directory.

Read alongside: council-loop.mjs, feature-loop.mjs, ultracode-fix.mjs, and autofix-swarm.mjs.

docs.title: The runtime contract
docs.text:
A workflow script is a pure coordinator. autofix-swarm.mjs states the contract most explicitly:

  • The first statement is a pure-literal export const meta.
  • The orchestrator body does zero real I/O. No fs, no child_process, no git, no Date.now(), no Math.random().
  • The body only sequences the injected primitives: agent(), parallel(), pipeline(), phase(), log(), and workflow(). It reads schema-validated returns, branches, and loops.
  • Every world-touching action, such as running tests or committing, happens inside an agent() prompt. Those agents hold the real tools.

This split keeps the orchestrator deterministic and resumable. The agents do the work. The script decides what happens next.

docs.title: The meta block
docs.text:
meta declares the workflow's name, a description, and its phases. The harness uses it for progress display and discovery.

export const meta = {
  name: 'ultracode-fix',
  description: 'Fix a task: sonnet explores, plan, implement, review loop',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Explore', detail: 'scout the codebase when the plan needs context' },
    { title: 'Plan', detail: 'produce a task-list fix plan' },
    { title: 'Implement', detail: 'apply each plan task' },
    { title: 'Review', detail: 'review, request fixes, loop until approved' },
  ],
}

Inside the body, call phase('Plan') when a phase begins. autofix-swarm.mjs adds a whenToUse field so a router can pick the workflow without reading its source.

docs.title: Defensive args
docs.text:
The harness may pass args as an object, a JSON string, or a bare task string. Every workflow here parses defensively at the top:

let A = {}
if (args && typeof args === 'object') A = args
else if (typeof args === 'string' && args.trim()) {
  try { A = JSON.parse(args) } catch { A = { task: args } }
}

Then derive named constants with defaults: const TEST = A.testCmd || 'npm test'. Clamp numeric knobs to safe ranges, as autofix-swarm.mjs does with maxIterations (3 to 6) and fanout (2 to 3).

docs.title: agent() with schemas
docs.text:
agent(prompt, opts) spawns one subagent and returns its result. Pass a JSON Schema in opts.schema to get a validated object back instead of prose. ultracode-fix.mjs builds its whole loop on two schemas:

const REVIEW_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  required: ['approved', 'findings'],
  properties: {
    approved: { type: 'boolean' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        required: ['file', 'summary', 'fixInstruction'],
        properties: {
          file: { type: 'string' },
          summary: { type: 'string' },
          fixInstruction: { type: 'string' },
        },
      },
    },
  },
}

Design each field for the orchestrator's next decision. approved drives the loop condition. Each finding carries a fixInstruction written to be self-contained, so it can go straight into a fix agent's prompt without extra context.

Other useful opts: label (log identity), phase, model, effort, and isolation: 'worktree' for a fresh git worktree per agent.

docs.title: Parallel versus sequential
docs.text:
Use parallel() for independent work, plain await for dependent steps. ultracode-fix.mjs runs plan tasks in dependency waves: sequential across waves, parallel within a wave.

const results = await parallel(wave.map(t => () =>
  agent(implPrompt(t), { label: `impl:${t.id}`, model: 'opus', effort: 'low' })))

council-loop.mjs runs its advocate and critic in parallel, then feeds both transcripts to a single arbiter. Fan out the lenses, then converge through one synthesis agent.

docs.title: Model tiering per role
docs.text:
Never let every agent inherit the top model. Assign a tier per role, with overridable defaults:

const MODELS = Object.assign(
  { diagnosis: 'sonnet', fix: 'sonnet', gate: 'sonnet',
    arbiter: 'opus', reviewer: 'opus', ledger: 'haiku' },
  A.model || {})

The pattern across these workflows: fan-out work (implementers, per-repo appliers, mechanical checks) runs on the cheap tier, synthesis singletons (planner, arbiter, reviewer) run on the deep tier, and bookkeeping runs on the cheapest tier. council-loop.mjs adds per-role effort overrides to bound spend on the expensive roles. See Model tiering for the full rationale.

docs.title: Budget and resume
docs.text:
Long loops must survive rate limits and token exhaustion. council-loop.mjs and autofix-swarm.mjs share the same machinery:

  • Limit-aware retry. A tryAgent() wrapper retries transient failures with backoff, but bails fast on a hard usage or rate limit. Retrying inside a blocked window burns quota and risks an empty result passing as a real one.
  • Budget floor. Before each expensive phase, check the optional budget global behind a typeof budget !== 'undefined' guard. Stop cleanly when budget.remaining() drops below a floor, rather than dying mid-phase.
  • Resumable stop. On a limit or budget stop, return { resumable: true }. The caller re-invokes with resumeFromRunId, and completed agent() calls replay from cache instead of re-running.

docs.title: Nesting workflows
docs.text: workflow() invokes another workflow one level deep. feature-loop.mjs delegates its whole review phase to council-loop.mjs. Invoke by absolute scriptPath: the name registry only resolves built-ins, and a relative path resolves against the project cwd. Pass a workflowsDir argument through so nested paths stay OS-correct.

docs.title: Design patterns
docs.text:
Adversarial verify. Never let the agent that wrote the code declare it done. ultracode-fix.mjs loops a reviewer against the implementers. council-loop.mjs goes further: an advocate argues for the change, a critic argues against it, and an arbiter issues the verdict. autofix-swarm.mjs adds a hard anti-gaming gate that rejects any candidate diff that touches test files or weakens assertions.

Loop until dry. Convergence is a checked condition, not a hope. council-loop.mjs re-convenes the council after each fix round until the verdict is an unconditional FOR with zero findings, bounded by maxLoops. ultracode-fix.mjs loops review and fix until approved is true, bounded by maxLoops. Every loop carries both a success condition and a hard iteration cap.

Champion promotion. When one fix would do, race several. autofix-swarm.mjs fans out 2 to 3 competing fix agents, each in an isolated worktree with a distinct strategy: minimal patch, targeted refactor, alternative root cause. A gate filters gamed candidates, then the orchestrator promotes one champion per iteration: the smallest passing diff in bug mode, the best metric in perf mode. Failures retire to a dead-ends ledger so later iterations never re-spend on them.

Critique before compute. autofix-swarm.mjs runs a council over candidate approaches before spawning any worktree. A shortlist debate costs a fraction of a wasted fan-out.

Branch pinning. Agents share one working tree across a long run, and the checkout a previous agent left behind is not trustworthy. council-loop.mjs injects a branch-pin instruction into every tree-touching agent: verify the branch first, and never commit or push to the parent branch. Encode safety invariants as injected prompt fragments, not as assumptions.

docs.title: Clip-path borders
docs.text: CSS border and box-shadow: inset do not produce visible borders on clip-path elements. A content background covers an inset shadow, and the clip-path cuts a border away. This page shows the technique that works.

docs.title: Wrapper-fill pattern (preferred)
docs.text:
Two nested clip-paths. The outer carries the border color, the inner carries the fill:

/* Outer: border color */
.panel {
    background: var(--border-color);
    padding: 1px;
    clip-path: polygon(
        12px 0, calc(100% - 12px) 0,
        100% 12px, 100% calc(100% - 12px),
        calc(100% - 12px) 100%, 12px 100%,
        0 calc(100% - 12px), 0 12px
    );
}

/* Inner: fill color */
.panel-content {
    background-color: var(--fill-color);
    clip-path: polygon(
        11px 0, calc(100% - 11px) 0,
        100% 11px, 100% calc(100% - 11px),
        calc(100% - 11px) 100%, 11px 100%,
        0 calc(100% - 11px), 0 11px
    );
}

The 1px gap between the outer (12px chamfer) and inner (11px chamfer) clip-paths creates a consistent border, including at the chamfered corners.

docs.title: Pseudo-element pattern (alternative)
docs.text: Same idea, but the inner clip lives on ::before with position: absolute; inset: 1px. This requires z-index management to keep content above the pseudo-element.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text: Wrong Why it fails box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px Content backgrounds sit on top of the shadow border: 1px solid The border sits outside the clip-path, so the clip cuts it ::before with backdrop-filter Blurs the content underneath, and z-index fights

docs.title: Council patterns
docs.text: The adversarial council is a review pattern built on real spawned agents, not role-played prose. This article describes the roles, the debate protocol, and the discipline that keeps findings honest. The repo's adversarial-council skill implements it.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A team of agents debates a motion: a decision, a plan, or a code change. Advocates argue for it. Critics argue against it. A Socratic questioner watches the live debate and probes any claim that skips its reasoning chain. An arbiter moderates and produces a structured recommendation: FOR, AGAINST, or CONDITIONAL, with cited rationale.

The questioner does not block the debate. It fires "Why?" at unsubstantiated claims in parallel, like a child asking "but why?" at the dinner table: relentless, parallel, and ultimately clarifying.

For code motions, all agents independently read the relevant files before the debate opens. Positions ground in what the code says, not what agents assume it says.

docs.title: Real agents only
docs.text: The debate must run as real spawned agents on a shared team, never as sections of prose in one response. A single model writing ADVOCATE and CRITIC headers argues with itself and converges early. Separate agents with separate contexts do not.

docs.title: Role persistence
docs.text:
Every council agent (advocate, critic, questioner, arbiter) must:

  • Maintain their assigned character for the entire debate.
  • Not drift toward consensus prematurely.
  • Not soften their position without a cited reason.

docs.title: Round protocol
docs.text:
Every message from a debate agent must:

  1. Start with exactly one header: the agent's role name (for example, ## CRITIC).
  2. Address the previous turn before introducing new points.
  3. Stay inside the round's scope. A rebuttal round is not a new argument round.

When rebutting a specific claim, name the agent, quote the claim verbatim, then present counter-evidence:

@ADVOCATE: "The cache layer adds no latency"
Counter: profiler output at cache.ts:142 shows 12ms overhead under load.

docs.title: Concession discipline
docs.text: Once an agent concedes a point, it must not re-argue that point in a later round. Concessions are permanent within the debate. The arbiter notes concessions in the recommendation to prevent re-litigation.

docs.title: Evidence grounding
docs.text:
Motion type Citation required Code file:line, plus a verbatim code excerpt or test output General A named source: doc URL, RFC, benchmark paper, or named prior art

The questioner challenges any claim that carries no citation. For code motions, every agent verifies a claim against the actual source before it enters any recommendation. The arbiter rejects any finding whose citation it cannot confirm.

docs.title: Arbiter obligations
docs.text:
The arbiter must:

  1. Summarize what each agent conceded, not just what they argued.
  2. Reflect questioner findings faithfully. Never upgrade an unsubstantiated claim to a finding.
  3. Issue FOR, AGAINST, or CONDITIONAL with cited rationale, not editorial opinion.
  4. Never invent findings to appear more thorough.
  5. Audit scope before compiling findings. Each finding must be directly about the motion, and the concern must not pre-date the motion. Drop findings that fail either test.

docs.title: Critical discovery threshold
docs.text:
An out-of-scope finding survives only when it clears a high bar:

Category Bar Examples Security OWASP Top 10 or equivalent SQL injection, auth bypass, exposed credentials, SSRF Data loss Corruption, silent deletion, unrecoverable state Missing rollback, unguarded cascade delete Compliance Legal or regulatory blocker Privacy-law violation, license incompatibility

Nothing else qualifies. That excludes performance, code quality, feature ideas, style, and tech debt. A critical discovery is an informational note only, not a fix target.

docs.title: Related skills
docs.text:
• council-supervisor adds heartbeat monitoring, stall detection, and checkpointing around the debate.
  • council-fix chains the council into a prioritised fix plan.
  • parallel-fix races competing fixes for the findings in isolated worktrees.

docs.title: Debugging protocol
docs.text: A discipline for diagnosing bugs before touching code. The core rule: no fix without a cited diagnosis.

docs.title: Hypothesis checklist
docs.text:
Before any diagnosis:

  1. Enumerate three or more hypotheses, with a one-line rationale for each.
  2. Gather evidence for all hypotheses before choosing.
  3. Mark the best-supported hypothesis only after the evidence is in hand.

Do not skip this step for "obvious" bugs. The obvious answer is often wrong.

docs.title: Evidence-first rule
docs.text:
Every diagnosis must cite:

  • file:line, where the defect lives
  • Log output, verbatim, not paraphrased
  • Stack trace, the relevant frames
  • Reproduction steps, the exact inputs that trigger the bug

If you cannot cite evidence, state the hypothesis as unconfirmed and gather more data.

docs.title: Diagnosis report template
docs.text:
Fill this template before proposing any fix:

## Diagnosis
**Symptom**: [observed behavior, exact, not interpreted]
**Hypotheses**:
  1. [H1 description]: [one-line rationale]
  2. [H2 description]: [one-line rationale]
  3. [H3 description]: [one-line rationale]
**Evidence Gathered**:
  - H1: [file:line / log / trace / repro]
  - H2: [file:line / log / trace / repro]
  - H3: [file:line / log / trace / repro]
**Root Cause**: [H#], [citation: file:line or log excerpt]
**Confidence**: high / medium / low
**Verification**: [how you confirmed the fix: test run, log check, repro attempt]

docs.title: Diagnosis agents
docs.text:
For non-trivial bugs (cross-file, unclear symptoms, or more than 15 minutes of investigation), delegate the diagnosis to a dedicated read-only agent:

  1. Spawn a diagnosis agent that never edits code.
  2. The agent generates hypotheses, gathers evidence, and fills the report template.
  3. The agent reports the root cause with citations.
  4. The main session reviews the report, then implements the fix.

Do not start fixing while the diagnosis agent is still gathering evidence.

docs.title: Timeboxing
docs.text:
• If a hypothesis is not confirmed within 10 minutes of investigation, pivot to the next.
  • After exhausting all hypotheses, escalate. Ask for more context or logs.
  • Never loop on the same hypothesis with a minor variation. That is thrashing, not debugging.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text: Anti-pattern What to do instead "It must be X" (no evidence) Enumerate hypotheses first Fix before diagnosis Fill the template before touching code Blame the framework Check your own code at the immediate callers first Assume the error message is literal Reproduce with a minimal repro case Skip hypotheses 2 and 3 Evidence often points to the non-obvious hypothesis

docs.title: Gherkin and specs
docs.text: The repo's feature-spec skill produces feature specifications that use two conventions: Gherkin for acceptance scenarios and MoSCoW for scope. This article explains both, for a reader who has never seen either.

docs.title: What Gherkin is
docs.text:
Gherkin is a plain-text language for describing software behavior as concrete examples. Each example states a starting condition, an action, and an expected outcome. The format is readable by anyone, and test frameworks such as Cucumber can execute it directly.

A Gherkin file is built from a few keywords.

docs.title: Feature
docs.text:
The top-level block. It names the capability and usually carries a short user story:

Feature: Password reset
  As a locked-out user
  I want to reset my password by email
  So that I can regain access to my account

docs.title: Scenario and Given / When / Then
docs.text:
A scenario is one concrete example of behavior. Its steps use three keywords:

  • Given sets up the starting state.
  • When performs the action under test.
  • Then states the expected outcome.
Scenario: Reset with a valid email
  Given a registered user with email "user@example.com"
  When the user requests a password reset for "user@example.com"
  Then a reset link is sent to "user@example.com"
  And the link expires after 60 minutes

And and But continue the previous keyword. Write one behavior per scenario. A scenario with two When steps usually hides two scenarios.

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
A Rule groups scenarios that illustrate one business rule:

Rule: Reset links are single-use
  Scenario: Using a link twice
    Given a reset link that was already used
    When the user opens the link again
    Then the page shows "This link has expired"

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Steps shared by every scenario in a feature move into a Background block, which runs before each scenario:

Background:
  Given a registered user with email "user@example.com"

docs.title: Scenario Outline
docs.text:
A Scenario Outline runs the same steps once per row of an Examples table. Placeholders in angle brackets take the row values:

Scenario Outline: Password strength validation
  Given a new password "<password>"
  When the user submits the reset form
  Then the result is "<result>"

  Examples:
    | password     | result   |
    | abc          | rejected |
    | correcthorse | accepted |

docs.title: MoSCoW scope
docs.text:
MoSCoW is a prioritisation scheme. The name comes from its four buckets:

Bucket Meaning Must-Have The feature fails without it. Each entry carries an acceptance condition. Should-Have Important, but the feature ships without it if time runs out. Could-Have (Nice-to-Have) Desirable extras. First to be cut. Won't-Have Explicitly out of scope, written down to prevent scope creep.

The value is in the disagreements it forces early. When everything is a Must-Have, nothing is.

docs.title: How the feature-spec skill uses them
docs.text:
The skill interviews the user section by section and fills a template. A finished spec contains:

  • Overview: user story, problem statement, and explicit out-of-scope exclusions.
  • Success condition: one sentence, "This feature is complete when [verifiable state]." Every later scope dispute refers back to it.
  • Scope: MoSCoW buckets. Must-Have entries pair a behavior with an acceptance condition.
  • Technical plan: affected components, data model changes, API contracts, and dependencies.
  • Acceptance scenarios: a Gherkin block with a happy path, edge and failure cases, and scenario outlines for parameterised cases.
  • Exit criteria: a checklist that includes "all Must-Have scenarios pass in CI."

docs.title: How to read a spec produced by these skills
docs.text:
1. Read the success condition first. It is the contract.
  2. Check the Must-Have list. That is what the implementation must deliver.
  3. Read the Gherkin scenarios as the test plan. Each scenario should trace to at least one automated test.
  4. Treat Won't-Have and out-of-scope entries as binding. Work that touches them needs a new spec.

The implement-spec skill consumes these specs and turns the scenarios into tasks for subagents.

docs.title: Claude Code hooks
docs.text:
Claude Code hooks are shell commands the harness runs around tool calls. They give you deterministic guard rails that do not depend on the model remembering an instruction. This article covers how hooks work, the design philosophy behind the hooks in this repo, and how to install them.

The scripts described here live in harnesses/claude-code/hooks/.

docs.title: How hooks work
docs.text:
Hooks are configured in ~/.claude/settings.json under the hooks key. Each entry names an event, a matcher, and one or more commands.

The main events:

Event When it fires Typical use PreToolUse Before a tool call runs Validate, warn, or block the call PostToolUse After a tool call completes Check the result, auto-format, reindex SessionStart When a session begins Environment health checks, context loading Stop When the agent finishes a turn Final verification, sync, cleanup

Mechanics:

  • The matcher is a regex against the tool name. "Bash" matches Bash calls. "Edit|Write" matches both file-write tools. An empty matcher matches every tool.
  • The hook receives the tool call as JSON on stdin. A Bash hook reads .tool_input.command. A file hook reads .tool_input.file_path. Most scripts here extract these with jq.
  • Exit code 2 blocks the tool call. For a blocking PreToolUse hook, write the reason to stderr. The harness surfaces stderr back to the model, which can then correct course.
  • Exit code 0 lets the call proceed. For PreToolUse and PostToolUse, plain stdout goes to the debug log only, and the model never sees it. To reach the model, print JSON with hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext for a note, or permissionDecision (allow, deny, ask) for a decision. SessionStart stdout is the exception: the model reads it as context.
  • A handler if field holds one permission rule, such as "if": "Bash(git commit *)". It checks each part of a compound command and keeps the hook off unrelated calls.
  • A SessionStart hook must never exit non-zero. It reports, it does not gate.

docs.title: Design philosophy
docs.text:
The hooks in this repo fall into three families.

Guard rails block actions that violate a convention or risk damage. Naming conventions, draft-PR merges, lint failures, and oversized files are all cheaper to stop before the fact than to unwind after. A guard rail prints a precise reason and an example of the correct form, so the model can retry correctly on the next attempt.

Auth safety removes a class of mistake entirely. When one machine holds two GitHub accounts, a push under the wrong identity is silent and hard to undo. A hook that switches the account to match the remote owner makes the mistake impossible.

Suggestion hooks nudge instead of block. They return the hint as additionalContext JSON and always exit 0. Each one carries a cooldown file so it does not fire on every matching call. The model stays free to ignore the hint when it has a reason to.

docs.title: Guard rails (PreToolUse, matcher Bash)
docs.text:
gh-check-before-create.sh enforces git and GitHub naming. Branch names must match <type>/<issue>-<kebab-description>. PR titles must follow conventional commits or a documented bracketed style. Both violations exit 2. Commit messages and short issue titles get warnings only. The hook also blocks merging a PR that is still in draft. With AGENKIC_MERGE_GATE=ask set, it asks the user before any other merge. It also warns before branch renames and issue relabels that can trigger repo automation. It only enforces naming in repos that carry an issue-branch-handler workflow, so ordinary repos pass through untouched.

lint-precommit.sh intercepts git commit and runs the project's linter. It detects the stack from manifest files: npm run lint and tsc --noEmit for JS/TS, ruff or flake8 for Python, go vet and gofmt for Go. The hook only checks. It never edits or stages files. Errors block the commit with the lint output and the command that fixes them.

large-file-check.sh blocks git commit when the tree carries any file over 100MB. GitHub rejects such pushes anyway, so failing early saves a wasted commit.

docs.title: Auth safety (PreToolUse, matcher Bash)
docs.text: pre-push-auth.sh intercepts git push, reads the origin remote URL, and switches the active gh account to match the owner. The owner-to-account mapping is a small case block you edit once. Unknown remotes pass through untouched.

docs.title: Suggestion hooks
docs.text:
agent-route-suggest.sh (PreToolUse, matcher Agent) fires when Claude spawns a subagent without an explicit subagent_type or model. It suggests the routing skills that pick a specialist and a model tier. When both fields are set, it stays silent: the caller made a deliberate choice.

context7-suggest.sh (PostToolUse, matcher Read) fires when Claude reads a dependency manifest: package.json, requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, go.mod, or Cargo.toml. It extracts the top dependencies and hints at a docs lookup before writing code against an unfamiliar library.

docs.title: Correctness checks (PostToolUse, matcher Edit|Write)
docs.text: python-syntax-check.sh parses any edited .py file with ast. A syntax error exits 2 with the line and message on stderr, which forces the model to fix the file before it moves on.

docs.title: Verification gate (Stop)
docs.text: stop-verify-gate.sh runs the project's .claude/verify.sh when Claude tries to end its turn. A failure blocks the stop and returns the output tail, so Claude keeps working until the check passes. On a second consecutive block it allows the stop, so it never loops.

docs.title: Environment health (SessionStart)
docs.text: preflight-check.sh prints [PREFLIGHT] warnings at session start: package-manager lock files, node availability, and stale git index.lock files. A healthy host prints nothing. It always exits 0. The model reads the report and resolves blockers before they surface mid-task.

docs.title: Not ported
docs.text: The source environment also runs hooks that are too personal to publish. They include vault sync and auto-push hooks for a private Obsidian vault. They also include semantic-index maintenance hooks for local services, an account-specific auth switcher, and plugin path normalizers. They follow the same patterns as the hooks above. They stay useful as categories even without the scripts. One example is a Stop hook that commits and pushes a knowledge base. Another is PostToolUse hooks that keep local indexes fresh after edits.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Copy the scripts into ~/.claude/hooks/ and make them executable:
mkdir -p ~/.claude/hooks
cp harnesses/claude-code/hooks/*.sh ~/.claude/hooks/
chmod +x ~/.claude/hooks/*.sh

  1. Edit pre-push-auth.sh and fill in your own remote-owner-to-account mapping. Skip the file entirely when you only use one GitHub account.

  2. Merge the fragment in harnesses/claude-code/settings.hooks.example.json into your ~/.claude/settings.json. The fragment wires each script to its event and matcher.

  3. Restart Claude Code. Hooks load at session start.

The scripts require bash, jq, and git. On Windows, Claude Code runs hooks under Git Bash, so the same scripts work unchanged.

docs.title: Model tiering
docs.text: When a workflow fans out many subagents, do not let every agent inherit the main session's model. Assign a model tier explicitly, per role. Token spend concentrates in fan-out stages, and putting the top model there is what exhausts a session budget.

docs.title: Role to tier mapping
docs.text:
The tiers below use generic labels. Map them to your provider's models: a top reasoning model, a strong mid-tier model, and a cheap fast model.

Role Tier Notes Thinker: workflow design, high-level synthesis, hard-to-diagnose root-causing Top Reserve for synthesis singletons and escalation only. Orchestrator: coordination agents, plan and spec composers, arbiters, revision singletons Top or strong mid Also the default reviewer tier when a review needs depth. Implementer: code writers, per-repo appliers, porters, mechanical API work Mid The fan-out tier. Most agent volume lives here. Reviewer: adversarial lenses, verification panels Top for subtle or high-risk changes. Mid for mechanical YAML and config verification.

docs.title: Escalation rule
docs.text:
Escalate an agent to the top tier only for high-level design or a hard-to-diagnose task. That means a root cause that survived a failed mid-tier attempt, cross-system reasoning, or the canonical fix others will copy.

Never put the top tier on a fan-out stage, such as N review lenses across rounds or per-repo appliers.

docs.title: In workflow scripts
docs.text:
// Synthesis or hard-diagnosis singleton. Escalate.
const spec = await agent(synthPrompt, { schema: SPEC, model: 'top' })
// Coordination, arbitration, deep review. Orchestrator tier.
const verdict = await agent(arbiterPrompt, { schema: VERDICT, model: 'top' })
// Fan-out: implement, apply, port, mechanical verify.
const results = await parallel(repos.map(r => () =>
  agent(applyPrompt(r), { schema: APPLY, model: 'mid' })))

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: The rule comes from a real failure. A 33-agent run once inherited the top model everywhere. It burned about 2M subagent tokens and hit the session limit. Review and apply fan-out on a mid-tier model is materially cheaper, with no observed quality loss on YAML and config work.

docs.title: Harnesses
docs.text:
The harnesses/ directory holds shareable configuration for five agent runtimes. Each subdirectory carries the settings, hooks, and wiring notes for one harness. The setup scripts symlink or copy these into place.

Harness Directory Config target Claude Code harnesses/claude-code/ ~/.claude/ (all platforms) Codex CLI harnesses/codex/ ~/.codex/ (all platforms) OpenCode harnesses/opencode/ ~/.config/opencode/ (Linux/macOS), %APPDATA%\opencode\ (Windows) Pi harnesses/pi/ Documented in its README when the config lands Hermes harnesses/hermes/ Documented in its README when the config lands

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
The primary harness. Expected contents:

File / dir Purpose settings.json.tmpl Shared settings: hooks wiring, statusline command, model defaults hooks/ PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, and Stop hook scripts agents/ Custom subagent definitions rules/ Shareable rules files loaded via CLAUDE.md includes

The skills live at the repo root under skills/ and install separately. The statusline scripts live under config/statusline/, and this harness wires them.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
Expected contents:

File Purpose config.toml.tmpl Model, approval policy, sandbox settings AGENTS.md Shared agent instructions

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text:
Expected contents:

File Purpose opencode.json.tmpl Provider, model, and keybind settings AGENTS.md Shared agent instructions

docs.title: Pi and Hermes
docs.text: Scaffolds only for now. Each README gains a file table when the first config lands.

docs.title: Adding a harness
docs.text:
1. Create harnesses/<name>/ with a README that states the config target path per OS.
  2. Add templates for any file that carries user-specific values. Use {{variable}} placeholders and document each variable in setup/answers.example.yml.
  3. Register the component in setup/components/.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The repo ships two installers with the same behavior:

Script Platform setup/setup.sh Linux and macOS setup/setup.ps1 Windows PowerShell

Both scripts symlink components from the repository into their target locations. They do not copy files, so a git pull updates everything in place.

docs.title: Interactive picker
docs.text:
Run the script with no arguments to get the picker.

./setup/setup.sh

.\setup\setup.ps1

The picker lists the available components: skills, workflows, each harness, and the shell configs. Select the ones you want. The script resolves each component's target path for your OS and creates the links.

Some components carry templates with {{variable}} placeholders. The installer prompts for each variable and writes the rendered file to the target.

docs.title: Non-interactive install with a profile
docs.text:
Pass --profile with an answers file to skip all prompts.

./setup/setup.sh --profile my-answers.yml

.\setup\setup.ps1 -Profile my-answers.yml

The answers file records which components to install and the values for template variables. Start from setup/answers.example.yml, copy it, and edit the values. A profile makes the install repeatable across machines.

docs.title: After installation
docs.text:
• Verify the links exist at the target paths. See Manual symlinks for the per-OS locations.
  • On Windows, symlink creation needs Developer Mode or an elevated shell. See the note in Manual symlinks.
  • Each harness has its own config target. See Harnesses.

docs.title: Manual symlinks
docs.text:
The setup scripts create these links for you. This page shows the manual commands for each OS, for when you want to link a single component by hand.

The examples link the skills/ directory into a Claude Code skills folder. Adjust source and target for other components.

docs.title: Linux and macOS
docs.text:
ln -s "$HOME/agenKic-hub/skills" "$HOME/.claude/skills/agenKic-hub"
  • The source path must be absolute. A relative source resolves against the link's directory, not your shell's directory.
  • Remove a link with rm, not rm -r. The target directory survives.

docs.title: Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink `
  -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills\agenKic-hub" `
  -Target "$env:USERPROFILE\agenKic-hub\skills"

Developer Mode

Windows restricts symlink creation. Either enable Developer Mode (Settings > System > For developers) or run PowerShell as Administrator. With Developer Mode on, a normal shell can create symlinks.

docs.title: Junction fallback
docs.text:
If you cannot enable Developer Mode, use a directory junction. Junctions need no elevation but only work for directories on local drives.

New-Item -ItemType Junction `
  -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills\agenKic-hub" `
  -Target "$env:USERPROFILE\agenKic-hub\skills"

docs.title: Copy fallback
docs.text:
As a last resort, copy the files. A copy does not track repository updates, so re-copy after each git pull.

Copy-Item -Recurse `
  "$env:USERPROFILE\agenKic-hub\skills" `
  "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills\agenKic-hub"

docs.title: Removing a link
docs.text:
# Linux / macOS
rm "$HOME/.claude/skills/agenKic-hub"

# Windows: removes the link or junction, not the target
Remove-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills\agenKic-hub"

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Each skill is a directory under skills/ with a SKILL.md that declares its name and trigger description. Install them by symlinking the skills/ directory into your harness's skills folder. See Install.

Skill Description adversarial-council Convenes advocate and critic agents to debate a decision, with a Socratic questioner and an arbiter who issues a structured recommendation. agent-route Recommends the optimal agent type for a task based on domain, complexity, and available specializations. brainstorm Collaborative design exploration before implementation. Asks clarifying questions, proposes approaches with trade-offs, and converges on an approved design. brainstorm-grill The relentless variant of brainstorm. Interrogates a plan down every branch of the decision tree and resolves each question with a recommendation. continuous-learning-v2 Instinct-based learning system that observes sessions via hooks, creates atomic instincts with confidence scoring, and evolves them into skills, commands, or agents. context-handoff Writes a handoff document that preserves decisions, failed approaches, and next steps before a session ends or compacts. context-resume Resumes work from a previous session handoff, verifying git state and re-reading key files. council-fix One-command alias for the full council review pipeline. Runs a supervised council and writes a prioritised fix plan. council-supervisor Wraps the council debate with a supervisor layer: heartbeat monitoring, stall detection, checkpointing, and structured results. cover-letter Writes a cover letter from a job posting in a configured personal voice and renders it as a LaTeX PDF. critique-loop Builds a rubric, runs independent critique rounds against it, or does both. croc-send Sends files and directories between machines using croc over tailscale. feature-spec Interviews the user section by section and produces a filled feature spec with Gherkin acceptance scenarios and MoSCoW scope. goal-writer Drafts Codex goals with evidence requirements, scope limits, and blocker conditions. Works in Claude and Codex. implement-spec Implements a feature from a spec file by routing tasks to subagents in dependency-aware parallel waves. insights-to-vault Archives a Claude Code Insights report into an Obsidian vault with a structured companion note. kilint Lints prose for AI-slop patterns without rewriting it: sentence length, passive voice, filler, and punctuation. merge-next End-of-work merge and advance skill. Squash merges the current branch, then checks out and rebases the next sibling branch. model-route Recommends the optimal model tier (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) for a task based on complexity and cost sensitivity. parallel-fix Spawns parallel agents in isolated worktrees to fix a bug with competing strategies. The smallest passing diff wins. release-notes-enricher Enriches git-cliff release notes with prose summaries by fetching linked PRs, issues, and commits from GitHub. repo-hooks Detects languages in the current repo and configures project-scoped hooks for type-checking, linting, and tests after edits. rubric-builder Defines concrete scoring anchors, weights, and required evidence. security-scan Audits Claude Code configuration for security vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and injection risks using AgentShield. ste-writing Rewrites prose that reads like AI output into a controlled house style, then scores the delta with kilint. visual-explainer Generates self-contained HTML pages that visually explain systems, code changes, plans, and data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
User Story: As the hub author, I want the canon hub to install my full environment, skills in groups, external rice components, and a guided onboarding path, so that a fresh machine reaches my complete setup from one entry point.

Problem: The canon hub has a flat 23-skill tree with one all-or-nothing manifest, a statusline that is only a README pointer to chrysaki-claude, no link to the dots or chrysaki repos, and no onboarding path. The Aurrigo hub now carries a richer, proven onboarding stack that the canon hub lacks.

Out of Scope: Any change to aurrigo-agentic-hub (frozen donor). Any sync mechanism between the hubs. A backport of the Aurrigo 816-line installer wizard. Absorbing statusline, theme, or dots content into canon (sibling repos stay sources of truth). A Chrysaki restyle of the onboarding deck.

docs.title: Success Condition
docs.text: This feature is complete when a fresh Linux or macOS machine, using only canon's README.md and docs/WALKTHROUGH.md, installs chosen skill groups and external components (statusline, tmux theme, dots) through setup.sh, attaches and detaches a tmux session, opens the command palette, and completes a first skill run, unaided.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text: # Question Raised By Resolved 1 None. All decisions resolved during brainstorm. - [x]

docs.title: Must-Have
docs.text:
• Skills regroup: skills/ moves from 23 flat dirs to four groups. Acceptance: every skill sits in exactly one group, no flat dirs remain.
  • core/: brainstorm, brainstorm-grill, feature-spec, implement-spec, merge-next, context-handoff, context-resume, agent-route, model-route
  • council/: adversarial-council, council-fix, council-supervisor, parallel-fix
  • writing/: ste-writing, kilint, visual-explainer, cover-letter
  • ops/: repo-hooks, security-scan, croc-send, release-notes-enricher, insights-to-vault, continuous-learning-v2
  • Per-group component manifests (skills-core.conf, skills-council.conf, skills-writing.conf, skills-ops.conf) replace skills.conf. Acceptance: the installer picker lists the four groups, and the skills step re-creates per-skill symlinks from the new group paths.
  • setup/relink.sh: one-shot script that repairs the vault symlinks (000-System/Skills/<name> targets) after the regroup. Acceptance: after a run, every vault skill symlink resolves.
  • Grep sweep: every skills/<name> reference in docs, manifests, and mkdocs nav updates to the group path. Acceptance: no dangling reference remains.
  • Installer growth on canon's own trunk (no wizard backport): a new manifest type=external with keys repo=, clone_to=, method=script|stow, run=. Apply clones or pulls the repo, then delegates to its own installer (method=script) or stows (method=stow). --dry-run prints the clone-and-run plan with no disk change. Acceptance: all three ext components install and dry-run cleanly.
  • Three external components:
  • ext-statusline: clones Kiriketsuki/chrysaki-claude and runs its installer. The config/statusline/ README pointer becomes a real install path.
  • ext-tmux-theme: installs the chrysaki theme into ~/.config/tmux/ and activates the {{tmux_theme_conf}} source line in the rendered conf.
  • ext-dots: clones Kiriketsuki/dots and applies it with stow.
  • Command palette: config/tmux/scripts/palette.sh plus the Section 8 binding, copied from the Aurrigo port. Acceptance: Prefix+Space opens the palette, and the script prints an install hint when fzf is absent.
  • setup/walkthrough.sh: canon adaptation of the Aurrigo script. Same five steps, checks driven by the new group and ext manifests. The statusline step is ext-aware: when ext-statusline is not installed, it offers the install instead of failing. Acceptance: completes on a machine without gum, resumes from saved state, --reset clears it.
  • docs/WALKTHROUGH.md: canon edition. Tiered path, command-first steps, the any-skill capstone, the 80 percent handoff trigger. The extras section documents the real ext-* components instead of prose pointers. Aurrigo-specific content does not carry over.
  • README landing rework: Start Here table with deep links into WALKTHROUGH tiers plus a short quick start above the fold, catalogue below.
  • docs/tips/: claude-md-curation, hooks, linters, multi-account, ported from the donor. All new docs pages wired into mkdocs.yml nav.

docs.title: Should-Have
docs.text: • kilint pass on all new and ported prose (under 1.5 violations per 100 words).

docs.title: Nice-to-Have
docs.text: • ext-* components report the cloned repo's HEAD sha in the install summary.

docs.title: Technical Plan
docs.text:
Affected Components: skills/ (regroup), setup/setup.sh, setup/components/ (four new skill manifests, three ext manifests, skills.conf removed), new setup/relink.sh, new setup/walkthrough.sh, config/tmux/tmux.conf.tmpl and new config/tmux/scripts/palette.sh, README.md, new docs/WALKTHROUGH.md, new docs/tips/ (4 files), mkdocs.yml.

Data Model Changes: New walkthrough state file ~/.cache/agentic-hub/walkthrough-state (one line per completed step). External manifests add four keys (repo, clone_to, method, run) to the flat key=value manifest format.

API Contracts: Not applicable.

Dependencies: gh (clone path), git, stow (ext-dots only), fzf (palette only, guarded), gum (optional), tmux. Sibling repos: Kiriketsuki/dots, Kiriketsuki/chrysaki (submodule of dots), Kiriketsuki/chrysaki-claude. All public.

Risks: | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation | |:-----|:-----------|:-----------| | Regroup breaks vault and ~/.claude skill symlinks | High | setup skills step re-links from group paths, relink.sh repairs the vault, both run in the same change | | Ext delegate scripts change interface upstream | Medium | manifests pin the run entry point, install summary prints the repo sha | | Walkthrough drifts from installer components | Medium | step checks derive from setup/components/ manifests, nothing hardcoded | | Donor content carries Aurrigo references | Low | grep sweep for aurrigo, , org URLs before commit |

docs.title: Acceptance Scenarios
docs.text:
Feature: Canon Hub Supercharge
  As the hub author
  I want grouped skills, external components, and a guided onboarding path
  So that a fresh machine reaches my complete setup from one entry point

  Background:
    Given a fresh Linux or macOS machine with git, tmux, and gh installed

  Rule: The installer delivers grouped skills

    Scenario: Group picker
      When the user runs setup/setup.sh
      Then the component picker lists skills-core, skills-council, skills-writing, and skills-ops
      And selecting a group symlinks each of its skills individually

    Scenario: Vault relink after regroup
      Given the vault symlinks point at the old flat paths

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
User Story: As the maintainer of both repos, I want a tool to generate the Aurrigo fork as an overlay of a pinned hub tag. Then a hub fix reaches the fork through a tag bump instead of a hand copy.

Problem: The private work fork is a hand-copied snapshot. Its workflows lack the hub's later fixes. For example, the fork council-loop.mjs differs from the hub copy in 740 diff lines, and it lacks the model clamp and the #26 gates. The fork installer is ahead of the hub in other places: --uninstall, a state ledger, --update, 32 template variables with detected defaults, and Nerd Fonts. Each side drifts on its own.

Out of Scope:

  • Any change to the fork repo in this PR. This PR delivers the spec only.
  • A path rename map between hub and fork. The overlay keeps hub paths as they are. A file that needs a different path stays fork-owned.
  • The plugin marketplace layout of #31. This spec keeps globs so that #31 only edits the include list.
  • Hub-to-fork sync of .github/. Each repo keeps its own CI and automation.
  • A merge of the fork config/ tree (statusline, tmux, zsh) into the hub.
  • GitNexus content in the fork. The user disabled GitNexus on 2026-09-11.

docs.title: Success Condition
docs.text: This feature is complete when one fork-sync apply run opens a fork PR that brings each selected hub file to the tag and passes the local gates. A second run against the same tag changes nothing.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
Every question has a recommended answer. The spec assumes the recommendation until the maintainer overrides it.

# Question Recommendation Raised By Resolved 1 The hub has no git tag. Its release.yml tags only on a merge into a release branch, and that branch does not exist. Where do tags come from? Extend version-bump.yml to push an annotated v<VERSION> tag after each bump commit on main. Tag v26.0.6.2 by hand once. Hub runners work, so the hub needs no fallback. Spec author [ ] 2 Where does the fork file map live? The hub is public and the fork is private. Split it. The hub holds the generic tool and the personal deny list. The fork holds .hub-overlay.toml with its include list and owned paths, so no Aurrigo path name reaches the public hub. Spec author [ ] 3 Allowlist or denylist for the export? Allowlist. The fork lists the hub paths it takes. The hub deny list stays as a backstop. A new hub file never reaches the fork until the fork lists it. Spec author [ ] 4 The fork renders {{workflows_dir}} in its workflow headers, but link_children symlinks workflows and never renders them. Keep the placeholder? No. Fork headers use the literal $HOME/.claude/workflows. The sync tool fails when a header file contains {{. Spec author [ ] 5 Should the hub carry its own CUSTOMIZE BEFORE FIRST USE headers? Yes. Generic headers help hub users too. The sync tool then swaps the hub header block for the fork header block by its marker line. Spec author [ ] 6 How does the fork bump its version while hosted runners are blocked by billing? The sync PR carries its own bump commit while .hub-overlay.toml sets version_bump = "local". Set it to "actions" when runners return, and the tool stops the bump. Spec author [ ] 7 Which branch type does a sync PR use in the fork? task/<n>-sync-hub-<tag>. The fork already uses task/ branches, and its bump rules map task/* to a patch bump. Spec author [ ] 8 The fork has an Aurrigo variant of release-notes-enricher in skills/aurrigo/. The hub has its own copy in skills/ops/. Which wins? The fork variant wins. The fork lists the hub copy under shadow, so the tool skips it and the two names never collide in ~/.claude/skills. Spec author [ ] 9 Do croc-send and insights-to-vault reach the fork? No. croc-send assumes a personal tailscale relay. insights-to-vault writes into a personal vault. Both go on the hub deny list. Spec author [ ] 10 Should the sync tool create the fork issue itself? Not in v1. apply --push requires --issue N. The tool prints the gh issue create command when the flag is missing. Spec author [ ] 11 Does the fork keep config/hooks/ or adopt harnesses/claude-code/? Keep config/hooks/ fork-owned until port step P7 lands the settings merge helper in the hub. Then adopt the hub harness and keep only gh-auth-switch.sh fork-owned. Spec author [ ] 12 Fork branch protection may require status checks that cannot run while billing blocks runners. Do not require hosted checks while billing blocks them. The PR body carries the local fork-sync verify report as the gate record. Spec author [ ]

docs.title: Sanitize Rules
docs.text:
The content gate runs on every hub-managed output file before the tool writes it. It also runs in the hub export-gate job on every hub file that the deny list does not exclude. Each pattern is an extended regular expression. The gate matches it without case.

Tier 1, deny (error everywhere). Personal data must never leave the hub. The patterns cover the personal home path, the vault name, vault-relative paths, the personal email, the personal SSH host alias and the personal config directory.

Tier 2, review (error in the fork export set, warning in the hub gate). Personal sibling repos are public, but the fork does not use them. The pattern covers the dots, chrysaki and chrysaki-claude repos.

Tier 3, reverse leak (error in hub CI on every hub PR). Work data must never reach the public hub through a port step. The patterns cover the private org name, the work GitHub account and the work SSH host alias. They also cover the work workspace path, internal hostnames and production service names.

Where the literal patterns live. The public hub must not hold the literal tier 1 and tier 3 values, because the list itself would leak them. The gate reads them from an untracked file, tools/fork-sync/deny-patterns.local, on the maintainer machine. Hub CI reads the same list from a repository secret, FORK_SYNC_DENY_PATTERNS. A missing list fails the gate closed.

Allowed lines: an origin: frontmatter line or a link that names Kiriketsuki/agenKic-hub. The hub is public, and the link is attribution. The bare word "Aurrigo" stays allowed, because the hub agent catalog names the Aurrigo Visual Explainer agent.

Path rules: the tool rejects a symlink, an absolute path, a path with .., and any output path outside the fork root. It skips binary files in the content gate and lists them in the plan.

Hub hygiene before the first sync (step M1). The scan on 2026-10-19 found five tier 1 hits in exportable hub files:

docs.title: Installer Port Steps
docs.text:
The fork setup/setup.sh has 816 lines and the hub copy has 498. The fork setup.ps1 has 612 lines and the hub copy has 228. Each step below is one hub issue and one hub PR. Each PR changes setup.sh and setup.ps1 together and adds a smoke test to setup/tests/.

The port keeps every hub safety feature: type=external, --force, clear_target, unique backup names, the failure count and the strict check for unresolved placeholders. The hub already has sed_escape, so it needs no port. The port must not bring back two fork defects: backup_if_real deletes an older .bak before it moves the file, and do_uninstall splits paths on spaces in a for p in $(...) loop.

Step Feature Detail P1 State ledger and --uninstall Record each link, copy, render, backup and external clone in a ledger. Write it to the state file named in setup/hub.conf. --uninstall removes a link only when it still points at the recorded source. It removes a copy or render only when its sha256 still matches. It restores each recorded backup by its exact path. It lists external clones and leaves them in place. --uninstall --dry-run changes nothing. P2 --update, --repair and stale prune Read the answers and components back from the state file. Re-render with no questions. Remove a link that the last run made and the new run drops. P3 Non-interactive flags and manifest keys --answers as an alias of --profile, --components LIST, --list-components, -y and --yes. Manifest keys default=yes\|no and group=. The picker shows desc. Skip .gitkeep. Set the execute bit on a rendered .sh file. P4 Data-driven brand and variables setup/hub.conf holds tool=, banner= and state_file=. A detect:<name> value in answers.example.yml selects a built-in detector: git_name, git_email, gh_user_1, gh_user_2, clipboard, node_bin. This replaces the fork VAR_KEYS list and default_for case, so setup.sh holds no variable name. P5 --render-skills Render a link_children tree into the target instead of a symlink. This mode substitutes known keys and warns on any other {{...}} token, because hub skills contain {{text}} and {{variable}} as prose. The strict check stays on for .tmpl files. P6 Nerd Fonts --fonts LIST, --no-fonts and the font picker. The ledger records each font directory. --uninstall lists fonts and leaves them in place, as the fork does today. P7 Hook settings merge helper (Should-Have) Move install-hooks.sh, install-hooks.ps1 and the fragment format into harnesses/claude-code/. Each helper merges the hook fragment into settings.json and skips an entry that already exists.

The fork answers file has 32 template variables plus the components and fonts keys. The hub file has 8 variables. Three hub names differ from the fork names: node_path and node_bin, accent_color and tmux_accent_color, claude_config_dir and personal_config_dir. After P4, setup.sh holds no variable name, so each repo keeps its own names in its own answers file and templates. Neither repo renames a variable.

docs.title: Sync Tool
docs.text:
Location: hub tools/fork-sync/.

tools/fork-sync/
  fork-sync              bash wrapper, runs fork_sync.py with python3 -I
  fork_sync.py           stdlib only, Python 3.11 or later
  never-export.txt       path deny list
  content-patterns.toml  tiers 1 to 3 and the allowed lines
  README.md
  tests/                 pytest, with a fixture hub and a fixture fork

CLI:

fork-sync plan   --fork PATH --tag TAG [--hub PATH] [--diff] [--json]
fork-sync apply  --fork PATH --tag TAG --issue N [--hub PATH]
                 [--push] [--bump patch|minor|major] [--allow-downgrade]
fork-sync verify --fork PATH [--pr-title T --pr-body FILE]
fork-sync gate   --hub PATH [--ref REF]
Command What it does Exit codes plan The dry run. It computes the output tree and prints one line per path: add, modify, delete, render or same. --diff adds a unified diff. It writes nothing. 0 in sync, 3 changes pending, 1 gate or input error, 2 usage error apply It does what plan prints, in a temporary git worktree of the fork. It commits on the sync branch. With --push, it pushes and opens or updates the fork PR. 0 done or in sync, 1 error, 2 usage error verify It runs every fork CI job locally, plus the lock check. 0 pass, 1 fail gate The hub-side content gate on every hub file that the deny list allows. 0 pass, 1 fail

Inputs:

  • --tag: an annotated hub tag that matches v<YY>.<n>.<n>.<n>[suffix]. The tool resolves it to a commit sha. It refuses a branch name or a bare sha.
  • --hub: a local hub checkout. The default is the repo that holds the tool. The tool runs git fetch --tags first, then reads files with git archive <tag>, so the working tree state of the hub does not matter.
  • --fork: a local fork checkout. The tool reads origin/main after a fetch. It ignores uncommitted work in that checkout.
  • .hub-overlay.toml and .hub-overlay/lock.json from fork origin/main.
  • never-export.txt and content-patterns.toml from the hub tag, not from the working tree. The rules then match the content they check.

Overlay config (.hub-overlay.toml in the fork, phase A):

schema = 1
hub_repo = "Kiriketsuki/agenKic-hub"
version_bump = "local"   # "actions" when fork runners return

[export]
include = [
  "workflows/autofix-swarm.mjs",
  "workflows/council-loop.mjs",
  "workflows/feature-loop.mjs",
  "workflows/feature-loop.md",
  "workflows/spec-loop.mjs",
  "workflows/spec-loop.md",
  "workflows/ultracode-fix.mjs",
  "workflows/ultracode-implement.mjs",
  "workflows/spec-loop.smoke.mjs",
  "workflows/workflows.smoke.mjs",
  "skills/core/**",
  "skills/council/**",
  "skills/writing/**",
  "skills/ops/**",
  "docs/patterns/**",
  "docs/tools/stream-launcher.md",
  "tools/stream-launcher/**",
  "tools/fork-sync/**",
]
exclude = []
shadow = ["skills/ops/release-notes-enricher/**"]

[fork]
owned = [
  "skills/aurrigo/**", "skills/meetings/**",
  "skills/project/**", "skills/fun/**",
  "setup/**", "config/**",
  "docs/tips/**", "docs/WALKTHROUGH.md", "docs/aurrigo-agentic-hub.md",
  "docs/deck/**", "docs/specs/**",
  "README.md", "AGENTS.md", "VERSION", ".gitignore", ".github/**",
  ".hub-overlay.toml", ".hub-overlay/**",
]

[render]
workflow_headers = ".hub-overlay/headers"
skill_origin = "origin: https://github.com/Kiriketsuki/agenKic-hub"

Lock file (.hub-overlay/lock.json, written by apply):

{
  "schema": 1,
  "hub_repo": "Kiriketsuki/agenKic-hub",
  "hub_tag": "v26.1.0.0",
  "hub_commit": "<40-char sha>",
  "tool_version": "1",
  "files": {
    "workflows/council-loop.mjs": {"sha256": "<hex>", "op": "render:header"},
    "skills/core/brainstorm/SKILL.md": {"sha256": "<hex>", "op": "render:origin"},
    "docs/patterns/hooks.md": {"sha256": "<hex>", "op": "copy"}
  }
}

Classification rules, checked before any write:

  1. A path in owned is fork-owned. An owned glob that also matches an export path is an error, unless shadow lists that export path.
  2. A path from the export set is hub-managed. The export set is the include globs, minus exclude, minus shadow, minus the hub deny list.
  3. When a tracked fork path is in neither class, the tool stops and names it.
  4. A hub-managed fork file whose sha256 differs from the lock is drift. The tool stops, names the file and gives two fixes: port the edit to the hub, or move the path to owned.
  5. A path in the old lock but not in the new export set gets a delete.
  6. Two skill directories with the same name in two groups is an error.

Outputs of apply:

  • A branch task/<N>-sync-hub-<tag> from fork origin/main, with the tag in kebab form, for example task/41-sync-hub-v26-1-0-0. The fork hosted runners cannot create branches, so the tool creates the branch by hand.
  • Commit 1: chore(sync): sync hub <tag>. The body names the hub commit and the counts of added, changed, rendered and deleted files.
  • Commit 2, only when version_bump = "local": ci: bump version to <X> [skip ci]. The bump follows the fork YY.Major.Minor.Patch[Suffix] rules. The default is a patch bump. --bump overrides it.
  • With --push: a push with --force-with-lease to the sync branch only, and one PR to fork main. The PR title is chore(sync): sync hub <tag>. The body holds Closes #N, the old and new tag, the hub commit subjects in that range for the exported paths, and the verify report.

Idempotency:

  • The output is deterministic. The tool sorts paths, keeps LF line ends, and keeps the file mode from the hub tree.
  • When the fork already matches the tag, apply prints "in sync", exits 0 and creates nothing.
  • When the sync branch already exists, the tool resets it to fork origin/main and applies again. The tool owns that branch, and no person commits to it.
  • When a PR for the branch exists, the tool edits its body. It never opens a second PR.
  • A tag older than the lock tag needs --allow-downgrade. This is the rollback path.

Preconditions of apply --push: gh api repos/<fork> succeeds with the active account, the fork issue N is open, and verify passes in the worktree. The tool never switches the gh account. When the check fails, it stops and prints the account it needs.

docs.title: Release Flow
docs.text:
1. A hub PR merges into main. The hub version-bump.yml bumps VERSION.
  2. The same workflow pushes the annotated tag v<VERSION> (step M0).
  3. The maintainer runs fork-sync plan --tag v<VERSION> --fork <path> and reads the plan. Exit 0 means nothing for the fork changed. The flow stops.
  4. The maintainer files a fork task issue from the fork template: "Sync hub v into the fork".
  5. The maintainer runs fork-sync apply --tag v<VERSION> --fork <path> --issue <N> --push. The tool creates the branch, both commits, the push and the PR.
  6. The maintainer reviews the PR. The user approves the squash merge, as for every merge.
  7. The squash commit on fork main carries the new fork VERSION. When version_bump = "actions", the fork bot bumps the version instead.

    8. A sync is optional per hub tag. The fork can skip tags, and the lock records only the last tag it took.

docs.text:
Feature: Fork Overlay
  As the maintainer of the hub and the Aurrigo fork
  I want the fork generated as an overlay of a pinned hub tag
  So that a hub fix reaches the fork through a tag bump

  Background:
    Given a local hub checkout with the annotated tag v26.1.0.0
    And a local fork checkout with .hub-overlay.toml on origin/main

  Rule: The plan is a dry run

    Scenario: Plan lists every change and writes nothing
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync plan with --tag v26.1.0.0
      Then each output path shows as add, modify, delete, render or same
      And the exit code is 3
      And git status in the fork shows no change

    Scenario: Plan stops on an unclassified path
      Given the fork tracks docs/new-note.md in no owned glob and no export glob
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync plan
      Then the exit code is 1
      And the output names docs/new-note.md as unclassified

  Rule: Sanitize rules block personal and private data

    Scenario: A personal path in an exported hub file fails the sync
      Given skills/core/brainstorm/SKILL.md at the tag contains a personal home path
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync plan
      Then the exit code is 1
      And the output names the file and the line

    Scenario: A deny-listed hub file never reaches the fork
      Given the fork include list contains workflows/**
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync plan
      Then workflows/financial-data-pipeline.mjs is not in the plan

    Scenario: A reverse leak fails hub CI
      Given a hub PR adds the private org name to setup/setup.sh
      When the export-gate job runs
      Then the job fails and names the line

  Rule: Apply is idempotent

    Scenario: First apply opens one PR
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync apply with --issue 41 and --push
      Then the fork has the branch task/41-sync-hub-v26-1-0-0
      And the branch has the sync commit and the version bump commit
      And one PR to main closes issue 41

    Scenario: Second apply on the same tag changes nothing
      Given the sync PR for v26.1.0.0 is merged
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync apply with the same tag
      Then the output says in sync
      And no branch, commit or PR appears

    Scenario: Drift in a hub-managed file stops the sync
      Given a fork commit edits workflows/council-loop.mjs on main
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync apply
      Then the exit code is 1
      And the output names the file and both fixes

  Rule: Render ops shape fork files

    Scenario Outline: Render op per file type
      Given the hub tag holds <file>
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync plan --diff
      Then the fork copy of <file> shows <result>

      Examples:
        | file                             | result                                    |
        | workflows/council-loop.mjs       | the fork header from .hub-overlay/headers |
        | skills/core/brainstorm/SKILL.md  | the origin line after the name line       |
        | docs/patterns/hooks.md           | the hub bytes unchanged                   |

  Rule: The installer ports keep both trees safe

    Scenario: Uninstall reverses an install
      Given setup.sh installed skills-core and config-tmux into a temp HOME
      When the user runs setup.sh --uninstall
      Then every recorded link and rendered file is gone
      And every recorded backup is back at its original path

    Scenario: Uninstall keeps a file the user edited
      Given the user edited a rendered file after install
      When the user runs setup.sh --uninstall
      Then the edited file stays in place
      And the output names it as changed since install

  Rule: The fork flow needs no fork Actions

    Scenario: Verify runs every fork CI job locally
      Given fork hosted runners are blocked
      When the maintainer runs fork-sync verify
      Then each fork ci.yml job runs on the local machine
      And the report lands in the sync PR body

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
User Story: As a user of the hub, I want one install command and marketplace updates. Hooks and workflows then wire themselves, and CI proves the package loads.

Problem: The hub ships through a symlink installer. Hooks need a hand merge into settings.json, and Windows needs a junction fallback. Every update means a re-run. Nothing validates the package, and no eval checks that a skill triggers or helps.

Out of Scope: The repo restructure itself. This PR delivers the spec only. Anthropic directory submission. claude.ai and Cowork support. Hooks for Codex, OpenCode, Pi or Hermes. A rewrite of any skill body beyond its references and configuration lines.
